title: Lesson 65: Enterprise AI Reference Architectures: RAG, Agent Platforms, and LLM Gateways
description: Reference architectures for enterprise AI: how RAG grounds answers in data, how an agent platform orchestrates work, and how an LLM gateway controls model access.

questions.question: In an enterprise AI reference architecture, what distinct job does each of the three core patterns perform?
options: RAG grounds answers in governed enterprise data, the agent platform hosts and orchestrates agents, and the LLM gateway controls model access, cost, and failover.
RAG controls model access and cost, the agent platform grounds answers in enterprise data, and the LLM gateway hosts and orchestrates a fleet of agents across teams.
RAG hosts and orchestrates agents, the agent platform routes every model call to a provider, and the LLM gateway grounds answers by retrieving passages from the index.
All three patterns perform essentially the same job of grounding, routing, and orchestrating, and differ only in the vendor that supplies each component.
questions.explanation: The three patterns compose but never overlap: RAG is the grounding subsystem for facts, the agent platform is the runtime for reasoning, memory, and tools, and the LLM gateway is the control plane for model access, cost, and failover.

questions.question: Why does model traffic need a gateway built for LLM calls rather than a general-purpose API gateway?
options: Request-count limits track capacity precisely because every model call consumes the same number of units regardless of its size and shape.
A general-purpose gateway cannot authenticate the callers that reach a model provider, so it must always be replaced before any model traffic is allowed.
Model cost and capacity are measured in tokens, so a request-count limit cannot track spend or fail over across providers.
Model providers refuse any traffic that has passed through a general-purpose gateway, so a purpose-built gateway is the only option.
questions.explanation: LLM cost and capacity scale with tokens, not request counts, so a request-count limit lets one user spend a token budget of any size and cannot apply semantic caching or multi-provider failover.

questions.question: When every application team integrates with model providers on its own, what capability does the enterprise lose, and what restores it?
options: It loses nothing at all, because each team calling providers directly is simpler, cheaper, and faster to operate than any shared infrastructure ever could be.
It loses the single governed point where budget, access logging, and model swaps are enforced, and a gateway restores one centralized control point.
It loses the ability to ground answers in enterprise data, which a gateway restores by retrieving and augmenting prompts before generation.
It loses the ability to store embeddings, which a gateway restores by maintaining the vector index for every consuming application.
questions.explanation: Direct provider integration leaves no one place to enforce budget, log access, or swap models, so a provider pivot becomes a rewrite of every caller; the gateway turns model selection into one governed, centralized decision.
